title: Taiwan Blocks Grab's Plan to Buy foodpanda Over Uber Links
summaryZh: 公平會否決Grab收購foodpanda台灣業務，憂與Uber關係削弱競爭。
summaryHi: ताइवान ने Uber से संबंधों के कारण Grab का foodpanda सौदा रोक दिया।
summaryEs: Taiwán bloquea la compra de foodpanda por Grab por sus vínculos con Uber.
summaryJa: 台湾公取委、Uberとの関係を理由にGrabのfoodpanda買収を不許可。
summaryKo: 대만, 우버와의 관계를 이유로 그랩의 푸드판다 인수 불허.
summaryEn: Taiwan blocks Grab's US$600 million foodpanda deal over its ties to Uber.
paragraphs: Taiwan's competition watchdog has blocked Singapore-based Grab Holdings from acquiring foodpanda's Taiwanese operations in a deal valued at roughly US$600 million, arguing that Grab's ownership ties to Uber could weaken competition in the country's food delivery market.

The sector is dominated by just two players, Uber Eats and foodpanda. Although Grab has no presence in Taiwan, Uber holds about 13.1 percent of its shares, and Uber's chief executive previously served on Grab's board. The Fair Trade Commission (FTC) feared this relationship would leave consumers with, in effect, a single dominant group.

Commissioner Shin Chih-chung told reporters that three commissioners voted to reject the deal, one supported approval with conditions and one stepped aside. He described the market as highly concentrated, with strong network effects and high barriers to entry.

Grab had proposed remedies, including diluting Uber's stake, restricting its board seats and limiting the flow of information between the firms. The FTC, however, doubted they would work in practice. Shin said Grab was free to file a new application, while Grab said it was disappointed and argued the deal would have benefited customers, couriers and restaurants.

A delivery workers' union praised the ruling, warning that weaker competition would give platforms more control over pay and commissions. The FTC also blocked a bid by Uber Eats for foodpanda Taiwan in late 2024.
Taiwan has said no to a big business deal. A company from Singapore called Grab wanted to buy foodpanda in Taiwan. foodpanda is a food delivery app. The price was 600 million US dollars.
Taiwan's Fair Trade Commission checks big deals. It wants shops and apps to compete in a fair way. On Wednesday, it stopped the deal.

Why? Uber owns a part of Grab. Uber also has Uber Eats, the other big food delivery app in Taiwan. The commission thinks Grab and Uber are too close. Then there may not be real competition, and prices could go up.
Grab said it was disappointed. But it can ask again. A union for delivery workers was happy. It says fewer companies could mean lower pay for riders.
Taiwan's Fair Trade Commission (FTC) has rejected a plan by Grab, a Singapore-based company, to buy the Taiwan business of the food delivery app foodpanda. The deal was worth about US$600 million.

Only two apps really control food delivery in Taiwan: foodpanda and Uber Eats. Grab does not work in Taiwan yet, so at first the deal might look harmless. However, the FTC was worried about Grab's links to Uber. Uber owns about 13 percent of Grab's shares, and Uber's boss used to sit on Grab's board.

Three of the FTC's commissioners voted against the deal, and one wanted to allow it with conditions. Another did not vote. A commissioner said the market was already very concentrated and that it is hard for new companies to enter it.

Grab had offered some promises, such as reducing Uber's share and limiting the information the two companies share. The FTC was not sure these would work. Grab said it was disappointed, but it is allowed to apply again.
The delivery workers' union welcomed the decision. It said less competition could give big platforms more power over riders' pay. In 2024, the FTC also stopped Uber Eats from buying foodpanda Taiwan.

Taiwan's competition watchdog has blocked Singapore-based Grab Holdings from acquiring foodpanda's Taiwanese operations in a deal valued at roughly US$600 million, arguing that Grab's ownership ties to Uber could weaken competition in the country's food delivery market.

The sector is dominated by just two players, Uber Eats and foodpanda. Although Grab has no presence in Taiwan, Uber holds about 13.1 percent of its shares, and Uber's chief executive previously served on Grab's board. The Fair Trade Commission (FTC) feared this relationship would leave consumers with, in effect, a single dominant group.

Commissioner Shin Chih-chung told reporters that three commissioners voted to reject the deal, one supported approval with conditions and one stepped aside. He described the market as highly concentrated, with strong network effects and high barriers to entry.

Grab had proposed remedies, including diluting Uber's stake, restricting its board seats and limiting the flow of information between the firms. The FTC, however, doubted they would work in practice. Shin said Grab was free to file a new application, while Grab said it was disappointed and argued the deal would have benefited customers, couriers and restaurants.

A delivery workers' union praised the ruling, warning that weaker competition would give platforms more control over pay and commissions. The FTC also blocked a bid by Uber Eats for foodpanda Taiwan in late 2024.

Taiwan's Fair Trade Commission (FTC) has vetoed Grab Holdings' proposed US$600 million takeover of foodpanda's local business, concluding that the Singapore-based firm's entanglement with Uber posed an unacceptable threat to competition in an already lopsided food delivery market.

At first glance, the deal seemed unlikely to alarm regulators, since Grab does not operate in Taiwan. Yet Uber, whose Uber Eats service is foodpanda's only serious rival, owns roughly 13.1 percent of Grab, and its chief executive once held a seat on Grab's board. In the commission's view, such ties could blunt any incentive for the two platforms to compete fiercely.

Commissioner Shin Chih-chung disclosed that the decision was not unanimous: three members voted to block the acquisition, one favoured conditional approval and a fifth withdrew from the case. Shin characterised the market as highly concentrated, shaped by powerful network effects and formidable barriers to entry.

Grab's proposed safeguards, namely shrinking Uber's holding, curbing its board representation and restricting information sharing, failed to convince the regulator, which questioned whether they could be enforced effectively. Grab voiced disappointment, contending the deal would have delivered innovation to consumers, couriers and merchants, though Shin noted that nothing prevents it from reapplying.

Labour advocates applauded the outcome, arguing that consolidation would hand dominant platforms greater sway over riders' earnings and commissions. The ruling echoes the FTC's 2024 rejection of Uber Eats' own bid for foodpanda Taiwan, a deal Uber later abandoned.

In a decision with significant implications for Taiwan's platform economy, the Fair Trade Commission (FTC) has prohibited Grab Holdings from acquiring foodpanda's Taiwanese arm for an estimated US$600 million. The regulator's central concern was not Grab itself, which has no operations on the island, but its financial and governance links to Uber.

Taiwan's food delivery sector is effectively a duopoly shared by foodpanda and Uber Eats. Since Uber possesses approximately 13.1 percent of Grab's equity and its chief executive formerly sat on Grab's board, the commission reasoned that the merger could substantially reduce rivalry between the two remaining platforms, ultimately to the detriment of consumers.

The ruling was reached by a majority: three commissioners opposed the transaction, one advocated conditional approval and another withdrew from the deliberations. According to Commissioner Shin Chih-chung, the market is characterised by high concentration, strong network effects and substantial barriers to entry, conditions that make anti-competitive behaviour difficult to reverse.

Although Grab offered remedies, such as diluting Uber's stake and restricting information exchange, the FTC was unconvinced that they would prove effective in practice. Grab expressed disappointment, maintaining that the acquisition would have generated innovative services, but it retains the right to submit a fresh application.

The decision was welcomed by a union representing delivery workers, which argued that diminished competition would strengthen platforms' leverage over wages and commissions. Notably, it mirrors the FTC's 2024 rejection of a similar bid by Uber Eats.
